etymology: Latin Quartus ("fourth"), a common Roman name often given to a fourth child or fourth-born. One of the brethren who sent greetings in Paul's letter to the Romans (Rom 16:23).
biblical_def: Quartus is a Christian brother at Corinth named in a single line of Scripture — the closing greetings of Paul's epistle to the Romans: "Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother" (Rom 16:23). Of Quartus we know nothing beyond his name and that one designation: "a brother." His Latin name ("fourth") suggests he may have been a Roman, perhaps of servile origin (such ordinal names were common among slaves and freedmen). Yet the Spirit of God saw fit to preserve his name and his greeting in the inspired and permanent Word of God, alongside the more prominent Gaius and Erastus. That is the quiet dignity of Quartus: an obscure believer of no recorded office, no recorded deed, no recorded word — remembered forever in Scripture simply as "a brother." He stands for the great multitude of ordinary, faithful, unremarkable Christians whose names are written not chiefly in the few verses of Scripture but in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27), and whose simple designation — brother, sister, member of the family of God — is honor enough. The naming of Quartus reminds the church that God's record is not the world's record: the world remembers the great, but the Spirit remembered "Quartus a brother," and that remembrance will outlast every monument of the mighty.
webster_summary: A Christian brother at Corinth named once in Scripture, in the closing greetings of Romans (Rom 16:23), simply as "a brother"; he stands for the great multitude of obscure, faithful believers whose dignity is their brotherhood in Christ.

corruption_summary: Quartus is corrupted only when his obscurity is despised — when the church values the named and prominent and forgets that the Spirit honored an unknown believer simply as "a brother."
corruption_paragraphs: Obscurity-despised. The world, and too often the church, prizes the prominent, the gifted, the named, and overlooks the obscure faithful. The single line that preserves Quartus is a rebuke to that instinct: the Spirit of God, inspiring the most theologically weighty letter in the New Testament, paused to record the greeting of a man we know only as "a brother." His brotherhood in Christ was honor enough to be written in the permanent Word. The church that learns from Quartus learns to honor the ordinary faithful member as God honors him — not for office or fame, but for being a brother in the Lord.

Quartus has no significant postmodern redefinition; the principal point worth recovering is the dignity Scripture gives to the obscure faithful. The Spirit's preservation of an unknown believer's name and brotherhood stands against every culture, including our own, that measures worth by visibility and platform. In God's book of remembrance (Mal 3:16), the obscure who fear the LORD are not forgotten.

etymology: Greek Sōpatros ("of a safe/sound father," or "saving father"), from sōs ("safe, sound") + patēr ("father"). Sopater of Berea, son of Pyrrhus, one of Paul's traveling companions (Acts 20:4).
biblical_def: Sopater of Berea, the son of Pyrrhus, was one of the seven or eight delegates who accompanied the Apostle Paul on his final journey toward Jerusalem, carrying the collection gathered from the Gentile churches for the poor saints in Judea (Acts 20:4). The list reads: "And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus." Each of these men represented a church or region that had contributed to the relief collection (1 Cor 16; 2 Cor 8-9; Rom 15:25-27), and they traveled with Paul as appointed representatives, ensuring the offering was handled with transparency and accountability (2 Cor 8:18-21, "providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men"). Sopater came from Berea, the city whose synagogue Luke had praised as "more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11). He is likely the same person as the "Sosipater" whom Paul calls his kinsman in Rom 16:21 (the names are variants). Sopater illustrates the early church's practice of inter-church partnership in mercy: the Gentile churches, having received spiritual things from the Jewish believers, ministered material things to them in return (Rom 15:27), and they sent trusted men to carry the gift with integrity. He is one of the named brethren who served the body of Christ across the divisions of geography and ethnicity, embodying the unity of the one church gathered from many nations.

corruption_summary: Sopater is corrupted only when the early church's careful, accountable practice of handling money in mercy ministry is forgotten, or when the named delegates of the collection are passed over as a mere travel list rather than a model of inter-church partnership.
corruption_paragraphs: Travel-list dismissal. The list of Paul's companions in Acts 20:4 reads, at a glance, like a mere itinerary detail. It is in fact a window into the early church's practice of mercy: these named men were the appointed delegates of contributing churches, traveling with Paul to carry the relief collection to Jerusalem with transparency and accountability. Paul deliberately involved trusted representatives so that no one could blame him in the handling of the abundance (2 Cor 8:20-21). Sopater and his fellow delegates model the church's care to handle money in ministry honestly "in the sight of men" as well as before God — a discipline the church neglects to its shame.

Sopater has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the model of inter-church partnership in mercy: the Gentile churches ministering materially to the Jewish saints from whom they had received spiritual things (Rom 15:27), the offering carried by named, accountable delegates. The unity of the church across ethnic and geographic lines, expressed in practical generosity handled with integrity, is the standing lesson of Sopater and the named brethren of the collection.

etymology: Greek Stephanas (likely a shortened form of Stephanophoros, "crown-bearer," related to stephanos, "crown, wreath"). The head of a household that was the firstfruits of Achaia, addicted to the ministry of the saints (1 Cor 1:16; 16:15-17).
biblical_def: Stephanas was a Christian at Corinth whose household holds a notable place in the New Testament: it was "the firstfruits of Achaia" (the first converts of that Greek province) and devoted itself wholeheartedly to the service of the saints. Paul names him three times in 1 Corinthians. First, in the matter of baptism, Paul recalls, "I baptized also the household of Stephanas" (1 Cor 1:16) — one of the few he personally baptized at Corinth, and a household baptism that figures in discussions of who is included in the church. Second and most fully, near the letter's close: "I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,) That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth" (1 Cor 16:15-16). The word rendered "addicted" (Greek etaxan heautous, "they appointed/devoted themselves") is striking: the household of Stephanas had voluntarily set themselves to the unglamorous, ongoing work of serving fellow believers, and Paul urges the church to submit to and honor such devoted servants. Third, Stephanas was one of three men — with Fortunatus and Achaicus — who came to Paul (likely bringing the Corinthians' letter and gifts) and "refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Cor 16:17-18), men whose service Paul says deserves acknowledgment. Stephanas thus models the devoted lay servant: not an apostle or a named office-holder, but the head of a household that gave itself to the constant, practical ministry of the saints, and was honored for it by the apostle himself. He embodies the truth that the church is held together not only by its appointed leaders but by the self-appointed devotion of ordinary believers who addict themselves to serving others.

corruption_summary: Stephanas is corrupted when the household baptism is pressed beyond what the text warrants in the credo-/paedobaptism debate, when his model of self-appointed lay service is forgotten, or when Paul's call to honor such servants is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Household-baptism over-reading. The baptism of "the household of Stephanas" (1 Cor 1:16) is cited in the paedobaptism debate as possible evidence for the baptism of infants in a household. The text does not say whether the household included infants, nor whether any were baptized apart from personal faith; elsewhere the same Stephanas's household is described as having "addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints" (1 Cor 16:15), which describes responsible, serving believers, not infants. The Reformed Baptist reading holds that household baptisms in Acts and the epistles describe households of believers; the text of Stephanas, far from settling the matter for infant baptism, describes a household actively serving Christ. The dictionary holds the credobaptist position; the household of Stephanas does not overturn it.

Stephanas has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the model of the devoted lay servant: a household that voluntarily "addicted themselves" to the ongoing ministry of the saints, and whom Paul commanded the church to honor and submit to. The church is held together not only by its appointed officers but by ordinary believers who set themselves to serve. Paul's instruction — "acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:18) — rebukes a church culture that honors platform and overlooks faithful, unglamorous service.

etymology: Latin Fortunatus ("blessed, fortunate, prospered"), from fortuna ("fortune"). A common Roman name, often borne by slaves and freedmen. One of three Corinthian believers who refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Cor 16:17).
biblical_def: Fortunatus was a Christian at Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Achaicus, came to the Apostle Paul (likely at Ephesus, bringing the letter and gifts of the Corinthian church) and refreshed his spirit during a difficult season of ministry. Paul writes: "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:17-18). Of Fortunatus himself we know only his name and this one service, but the service was real and valued: in supplying "that which was lacking" from the Corinthians (perhaps practical support, perhaps simply their presence and fellowship), these three men ministered to the apostle's weary spirit. The phrase "they have refreshed my spirit" is precious: even the great apostle, who poured himself out for the churches, needed and received refreshment from ordinary believers. His Latin name, common among the servile classes, again suggests a man of humble origin, perhaps a slave or freedman, whose service to the apostle was nonetheless recorded forever in the inspired Word. Fortunatus models the ministry of refreshment — the often-overlooked grace of being a refreshment to weary servants of Christ. Paul elsewhere prays for the household of Onesiphorus because "he oft refreshed me" (2 Tim 1:16), and the writer to Philemon rejoices that "the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee" (Philem 7). To refresh the spirit of a weary laborer is a real and commendable ministry, and Fortunatus is forever named among those who did it.

corruption_summary: Fortunatus is corrupted only when the ministry of refreshment is undervalued — when the church forgets that even the strongest servants of Christ need refreshing, and that to be a refreshment to the weary is a real and recorded grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Refreshment-undervalued. The ministry of Fortunatus was simple: he, with two others, came to Paul and refreshed his spirit. In a results-obsessed church culture that prizes visible achievement, the grace of merely refreshing a weary laborer can seem too small to notice. Scripture notices it. Paul names Fortunatus forever for this service; he prays mercy on Onesiphorus's house because "he oft refreshed me" (2 Tim 1:16); Philemon is praised because the saints' hearts are refreshed by him (Philem 7). The faithful messenger refreshes the soul of those who send him "as the cold of snow in the time of harvest" (Prov 25:13). To refresh the weary is a ministry the Lord records and rewards.

Fortunatus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the value Scripture places on the ministry of refreshment. Even the great apostle, pouring himself out for the churches, needed refreshment and received it from ordinary believers of humble name. The church that learns from Fortunatus learns to honor and to practice the grace of refreshing weary servants of Christ — pastors, missionaries, and laborers who, like Paul, need the cold of snow in the time of harvest.

etymology: Greek/Latin Achaicus ("belonging to Achaia, a man of Achaia"), from the Roman province of Achaia (southern Greece). A common name, sometimes given to a slave from that region. One of three Corinthians who refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Cor 16:17).
biblical_def: Achaicus was a Christian at Corinth who, with Stephanas and Fortunatus, came to the Apostle Paul and refreshed his spirit, as recorded in the closing of 1 Corinthians: "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:17-18). His name means "a man of Achaia," the Roman province of southern Greece in which Corinth lay; such regional names were sometimes given to slaves identified by their place of origin, suggesting Achaicus may have been a freedman or slave. He is named together with Fortunatus (another humble Roman name) and Stephanas (whose household was the firstfruits of Achaia), and the three appear to have formed a delegation from the Corinthian church to Paul, likely carrying the letter to which 1 Corinthians is in part a reply, and supplying in person what the distance had left lacking. Achaicus shares fully in the honor Paul gives the three: they refreshed his spirit, and the church is commanded to acknowledge such men. Of his particular character, deeds, or later life, Scripture says nothing — he is one of the obscure faithful, named for a single, valued service. He stands, with Quartus, Fortunatus, and the other named brethren, for the great company of ordinary believers whose service to Christ and to His servants the Spirit of God saw fit to record in the permanent Word, that the church might honor them and learn from them the grace of practical, refreshing, self-giving service.

corruption_paragraphs: Obscure-faithful despised. Achaicus is one of the many believers in Scripture known by a single mention and a single service. The instinct of the fallen heart, and of much of church culture, is to honor the prominent and overlook the obscure. Scripture rebukes the instinct: "God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints" (Heb 6:10). Achaicus ministered to the saints and to the apostle; God did not forget it, but recorded his name in the permanent Word. The church that learns from Achaicus learns to value the humble servant as God values him.

Achaicus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the dignity Scripture gives to obscure, practical, self-giving service. Achaicus, of humble name and no recorded office, refreshed the spirit of the apostle and ministered to the saints, and is named forever for it. Like Quartus the brother and Fortunatus the refresher, he stands for the great company of ordinary believers whose labour of love God does not forget (Heb 6:10).

etymology: Greek Apphia, likely of Phrygian origin (a term of endearment or a regional name common in Asia Minor). A Christian woman addressed in Paul's letter to Philemon (Philem 2), traditionally understood to be Philemon's wife.
biblical_def: Apphia was a Christian woman at Colossae addressed by name in the opening of Paul's letter to Philemon: "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer, And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house" (Philem 1-2). She is traditionally and most plausibly understood to be the wife of Philemon, the master of the runaway slave Onesimus on whose behalf the whole letter pleads. The naming of Apphia is significant for several reasons. First, it shows that the deeply personal letter concerning Onesimus was not Philemon's private affair alone: his wife (and Archippus, perhaps their son, and the church meeting in their house) were all addressed, because the reception of the returning slave-now-brother would touch the whole household and the whole congregation. Second, Apphia's inclusion honors the place of the Christian wife and mother in the life of the household church — she is "our beloved Apphia," a sister addressed with affection and reckoned a party to the gospel matter at hand. The letter to Philemon is the New Testament's great case study in how the gospel transforms the master-slave relationship from within: Paul does not command Philemon to free Onesimus, but appeals to him to receive the returning slave "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (Philem 16). Apphia, as the mistress of the household, would have to live out that transformation daily — receiving the man who had wronged her household as a brother in Christ. Her naming reminds the church that the gospel's reconciling work is wrought not only in grand principle but in the concrete relationships of particular households, where particular women and men must extend the forgiveness and brotherhood the gospel commands.
webster_summary: A Christian woman at Colossae addressed by name in Paul's letter to Philemon (Philem 2), traditionally Philemon's wife; her inclusion shows the gospel's reconciling work touching the whole household, and honors the Christian wife's place in the household church.

corruption_summary: Apphia is corrupted when her naming is overlooked as incidental, when the household-transforming power of the gospel in Philemon is reduced to a private legal matter, or when the place of the Christian woman in the household church is diminished.
corruption_paragraphs: Incidental-naming dismissal. Apphia's name can be passed over as a mere courtesy greeting. Its inclusion is purposeful: Paul addresses Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the whole church in the house, because the reception of Onesimus as a brother was not Philemon's private decision but a matter touching the whole household and congregation. By naming Apphia (the wife and mistress of the house), Paul signals that she too is a party to the gospel reconciliation, who would live out daily the brotherhood the letter commands. Her naming honors the Christian wife as a real participant in the gospel life of the household, not a silent appendage.

Apphia has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the way the gospel transforms household relationships from within, and the place of the Christian wife in that transformation. The letter to Philemon does not abolish the master-slave structure by decree but dissolves its tyranny from the inside, requiring the master (and his wife Apphia) to receive the returning slave as "a brother beloved" (Philem 16). Apphia stands for every Christian woman called to extend, in the concrete relationships of her own household, the reconciliation and brotherhood the gospel commands.
roots_summary: A Christian woman at Colossae addressed by name in Paul's letter to Philemon (Philem 2), traditionally Philemon's wife; her naming shows the gospel's reconciling work touching the whole household and honors the Christian wife in the household church.

etymology: Greek Nympha (feminine) or Nymphas (masculine); the manuscripts differ on the gender. Related to nymphē ("bride, young woman"). A believer in Laodicea (or nearby) in whose house a church met (Col 4:15).
biblical_def: Nympha was a believer in the region of Laodicea in whose house a church gathered, named in the closing greetings of Paul's letter to the Colossians: "Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house" (Col 4:15). The Greek manuscripts differ on whether the name is feminine (Nympha) or masculine (Nymphas), and correspondingly on whether the house is "her house" or "his house" — a textual question that does not affect the doctrine but reflects the early uncertainty; many modern texts read the feminine, "Nympha... her house." Whether man or woman, Nympha holds the significant distinction of being one of several New-Testament believers in whose homes the early church met: the church in the house of Priscilla and Aquila (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19), the church in the house of Philemon (Philem 2), and the church in the house of Nympha (Col 4:15). These "house churches" were the ordinary form of Christian assembly in the apostolic age, before the church had buildings of its own: believers gathered in the homes of members able to host them, for the reading of Scripture, prayer, the Lord's Supper, and fellowship. To open one's home to the church was a real and costly service — it meant hospitality, expense, risk in times of persecution, and the disruption of one's household for the sake of the gathered saints. Nympha did this, and is named forever for it. If, as many hold, Nympha was a woman, she joins Priscilla, Lydia, Phoebe, and others among the women whose homes, resources, and labor advanced the early church — honored not by holding the teaching office (which Scripture reserves to qualified men) but by the indispensable ministries of hospitality, support, and service that the gospel opens to all the saints. The naming of Nympha reminds the church of the foundational ministry of Christian hospitality — the opening of homes for the gathering and good of God's people.

corruption_summary: Nympha is corrupted when the house-church and the ministry of hospitality are forgotten, when the textual question of the name's gender is made a battleground for agendas the text does not serve, or when the indispensable supporting ministries of the saints are undervalued beside the teaching office.
corruption_paragraphs: Hospitality-forgotten. The house churches of the apostolic age — in the homes of Priscilla and Aquila, Philemon, and Nympha — depended on believers willing to open their homes for the gathering of the saints. This was costly hospitality: expense, disruption, and in times of persecution real danger. Scripture commands hospitality of all believers (Rom 12:13; 1 Pet 4:9; Heb 13:2), and the named house-church hosts model it at the foundation of the church's life. A church culture that has professionalized and outsourced hospitality, and that no longer opens homes for the good of God's people, has lost something the early church held precious. Nympha opened a home; the church should learn the grace again.

Gender-debate over-reading. The textual question of whether the name is Nympha (feminine) or Nymphas (masculine) has been pressed into modern debates over women's ministry, with some eager to read "a woman leading a house church" as warrant for women in the teaching/governing office. The text will not bear the weight: hosting a church in one's home is the ministry of hospitality, not the holding of the teaching office, which Scripture reserves to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). If Nympha was a woman, she joins the honored company of women whose homes, resources, and labor served the church — a ministry the dictionary gladly honors, distinct from the eldership the New Testament orders otherwise. The dictionary holds the complementarian position; the house of Nympha neither establishes nor overturns it, because hosting a gathering is not the same as holding the office.

etymology: Latin Secundus ("second"), a common Roman ordinal name, often given to a second child or borne by slaves and freedmen. A Thessalonian believer who accompanied Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4).
biblical_def: Secundus was a believer from Thessalonica who, with Aristarchus, represented the Thessalonian church among the delegates accompanying the Apostle Paul on his final journey toward Jerusalem with the relief collection: "And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus" (Acts 20:4). Of Secundus himself Scripture records only his name, his city, and his inclusion in this delegation; his Latin ordinal name ("second") suggests, like Quartus ("fourth") and Tertius ("third"), that he may have been a Roman of humble or servile background, identified by birth-order in the common manner of the servile classes. Yet he was chosen as one of the trusted men to represent his church in carrying the offering to Jerusalem — a real responsibility, for the collection was a substantial sum gathered from the Gentile churches for the poor saints in Judea, and Paul was careful that it be handled transparently by accountable delegates (2 Cor 8:18-21). Secundus thus stands among the named brethren of the collection — ordinary believers entrusted with a sacred stewardship, who traveled with the apostle through danger (Paul went up to Jerusalem knowing bonds and afflictions awaited him, Acts 20:23) to minister to the unity of the church. His name, like the names of Quartus, Tertius, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, is one of the many humble Roman names the Spirit preserved in Scripture — a quiet testimony that in Christ "there is neither Greek nor Jew... bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all" (Col 3:11), and that the church was built, under God, by the faithful service of countless ordinary believers whose names the world would never have remembered but God did not forget.

corruption_summary: Secundus is corrupted only when the obscure faithful are despised, when the named delegates of the collection are read as a mere travel list, or when the church forgets that it was built by the service of countless ordinary believers whose names God preserved.
corruption_paragraphs: Obscure-faithful despised. Secundus, like Quartus and Tertius, bears a humble Roman ordinal name and is known by a single mention. The world remembers the great; the Spirit of God preserved the names of these obscure servants. Secundus was trusted to represent his church and carry the sacred offering through danger to Jerusalem — a real stewardship. The church that learns from him learns that the body of Christ is built not chiefly by the famous few but by the faithful service of the many, whose names, unknown to the world, are written in heaven (Luke 10:20) and, for a few of them, preserved forever in the Word.

Secundus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the dignity of the obscure faithful and the model of accountable stewardship in the church's mercy ministry. Secundus was chosen by his church to travel with Paul and the collection (cf. 2 Cor 8:19) — a trust handled transparently. His humble name, preserved in Scripture, testifies that in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Col 3:11), and that God does not forget the service of the lowly.

etymology: Greek Karpos ("fruit"). A believer at Troas with whom Paul left his cloak and books (2 Tim 4:13).
biblical_def: Carpus was a believer at Troas in whose house the Apostle Paul had left his cloak, his books, and especially the parchments — a detail preserved in one of the most poignant verses of Paul's final letter: "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments" (2 Tim 4:13). Of Carpus we know only his name, his city, and that Paul trusted him to keep his belongings. Yet the verse in which he appears is precious for what it reveals of the aged apostle near the end of his life. Writing from a Roman prison, awaiting execution, Paul asks Timothy to bring three things: his cloak (the heavy traveling cloak he would need against the cold of the Roman winter in his dungeon), his books, and especially the parchments (likely portions of the Scriptures or his own writings). The request is intensely human and deeply instructive: the apostle who had written half the New Testament, facing death, still wanted his cloak for warmth and his books and Scriptures for study and comfort. He did not consider that, having attained such heights of revelation and being so near glory, he was beyond the need of the Word; to the end he wanted the parchments — "especially the parchments." Carpus had faithfully kept these things, and Paul trusted him to have done so. The detail testifies both to the reality of the apostle's human need and to the value he placed on the Scriptures to his dying day, and it preserves forever the name of an obscure believer at Troas who had simply, faithfully, kept the things entrusted to him. Carpus stands for the humble faithfulness of keeping what is entrusted — a small service, perhaps, but one the Spirit of God saw fit to record.

corruption_summary: Carpus is corrupted only when the precious human detail of 2 Timothy 4:13 is overlooked, when the apostle's dying love of the Scriptures is missed, or when the humble service of keeping a trust is despised as too small to matter.
corruption_paragraphs: Precious-detail overlooked. The mention of Carpus and the cloak is easily skimmed as an incidental closing request. It is one of the most human and instructive verses in Paul's writings. The apostle, in a cold Roman dungeon, near execution, asks for his cloak against the winter, and for his books and "especially the parchments" — the Scriptures. Here is a man who had been caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor 12), who had written letters that are themselves Scripture, who was about to depart and be with Christ — and still he wanted the parchments to the end. The verse rebukes any notion that one can outgrow the need of the Word. Paul loved the Scriptures to his dying day; so should we.

Carpus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is twofold: the apostle's lifelong, dying love of the Scriptures ("especially the parchments"), and the humble faithfulness of Carpus in keeping what was entrusted to him. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). Carpus kept a cloak and some books; the Spirit recorded his name. The smallest faithful service, the keeping of a small trust, is not beneath the notice of God.

etymology: Greek Alexandros ("defender of men," from alexō, "to defend," + anēr, "man"); the coppersmith (Greek chalkeus, a worker in copper or bronze/metal) distinguishes him from others named Alexander. An adversary who did Paul much evil (2 Tim 4:14).
biblical_def: Alexander the coppersmith was an adversary of the Apostle Paul who did him much harm, named in the closing warnings of Paul's final letter: "Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words" (2 Tim 4:14-15). He stands in this batch of the named brethren as a deliberate foil — for the Spirit of God recorded not only the names of the faithful who refreshed and served the apostle, but also the name of one who opposed and harmed him. The designation "the coppersmith" (a worker in metal) distinguishes him from other men named Alexander in the New Testament (the Alexander of Acts 19:33 at Ephesus; the Alexander delivered to Satan in 1 Tim 1:20, who may or may not be the same man). Paul's words about him are sober and instructive. First, he names the harm plainly: Alexander "did me much evil" and "greatly withstood our words" — opposing not merely Paul personally but the gospel message Paul preached. Second, Paul commits the matter to God's justice rather than taking private vengeance: "the Lord reward him according to his works" — an echo of the Scriptural principle that vengeance belongs to the Lord (Rom 12:19; Deut 32:35), not to the wronged servant. Third, Paul warns Timothy to beware of him, for the danger was ongoing. Alexander thus illustrates several sober truths: that faithful gospel ministry will make real enemies (2 Tim 3:12, "all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution"); that the right response to those who do us evil is to commit the matter to God's justice rather than to repay evil for evil; and that the church must be warned against those who withstand the truth. The dictionary includes Alexander among the named brethren as the necessary shadow side of the picture: the Spirit's record is honest, preserving the names of opponents as well as helpers, that the church might know both whom to honor and whom to beware.
webster_summary: An adversary who did Paul much evil and greatly withstood the gospel (2 Tim 4:14-15); the deliberate foil among the named brethren; illustrates that faithful ministry makes enemies, that vengeance belongs to the Lord, and that the church must beware opponents of the truth.

corruption_summary: Alexander the coppersmith is corrupted when Paul's committal of the matter to God is read as petty cursing, when the reality that faithful ministry makes enemies is denied, or when the church's duty to beware opponents of the truth is softened into a false tolerance.
corruption_paragraphs: Vengeance-misread. Paul's words — "the Lord reward him according to his works" — are sometimes read as a petty, vindictive curse unworthy of an apostle. The opposite is true: Paul is NOT taking private vengeance; he is committing the wrong to the just Judge, in exact accordance with the Scriptural principle, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19; Deut 32:35). To hand a wrong over to God's justice is the alternative to personal revenge, not a form of it. The wronged servant of Christ does not repay evil for evil; he entrusts the matter to the God who judges righteously (1 Pet 2:23, as Christ Himself did). Paul's words model the right response to those who do us evil: not retaliation, but committal to God.

Enemies-denied misreading. A sentimental Christianity imagines that faithful, loving gospel ministry will win universal goodwill, and is scandalized when a minister makes real enemies. Scripture is more honest: "all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12). Alexander did Paul much evil and greatly withstood the gospel; the apostle warns Timothy to beware of him. Faithful ministry, because it confronts sin and proclaims an exclusive Christ, will provoke opposition, and the church must be warned against those who withstand the truth. The naming of Alexander, among the names of the faithful, is the Spirit's honest reminder that the church has both helpers to honor and adversaries to beware.
